rows.settles: AI starts speeding up its own invention if independent tests show agents doing more than a day of research work for each day a person puts in, and needing a person's help on long tasks less than half the time.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge of how fast factories, supply chains and robot hardware scale. The scenario needs superintelligence first and then an industrial build-out far faster than anything seen, all inside three years, and the first step already looks late. The strongest point for it is that humanoid robot output is growing quickly from a tiny base, but that is ordinary industrial growth, not an economy of robot factories.

rows.line: The race ending of AI 2027 has special economic zones filling with robot factories from 2028, with a robot economy covering them by early 2030.

judgement.reason: The task length agents complete reliably has been growing fast, and extending the reliable-horizon trend through 2027 gets to tasks of some weeks. The bar here is much higher: any coding task of the best lab engineer, far faster and cheaper, and the gap between the reliable horizon and the headline horizon has not closed. The authors themselves moved their medians later. The case for it is that the trend has repeatedly beaten sceptics and coding is where labs concentrate effort.

judgement.reason: A superhuman researcher needs a superhuman coder first plus research taste, and the coder milestone itself looks later than 2027. Self-reported lab figures show agents doing much research legwork, but people still step in on about as many long tasks as not, and no outside test shows an agent beating top researchers. rows.line: The AI 2027 scenario placed a superhuman AI researcher, one that outdoes the best people at AI research, at around September 2027.

judgement.reason: Judged as whether the catastrophe happens, this is unlikely, which is also what his low odds say. The judgement rests on general knowledge: labs do catch bad behaviour in testing, many actors would have to fail at once, and extinction-level outcomes need AI to gain decisive physical power. What cuts the other way is that control methods have never been tested on systems smarter than their makers, so the risk is small but real.

rows.line: Scott Alexander puts his chance of AI doom at about one in five, the lowest estimate among the authors of AI 2027.

judgement.reason: The test is an independent finding that an OpenAI system beats people at most economically valuable work by the end of 2026, and under three months remain. Outside tests show agents reliably finishing tasks of a few hours, not whole jobs, and Altman himself said the system was not there yet. A declaration by the lab is quite possible, but that would not meet the test.

rows.line: Sam Altman told TIME that OpenAI would have an internal system he would call AGI before the end of 2026, while conceding it was not there yet.

judgement.reason: During 2026 frontier models were credited with proofs of open mathematical problems and with useful research ideas, and several mathematicians have said the machine supplied the key step. That is enough for the call as loosely worded, a judgement from general knowledge. The strongest objection is that people still choose the problems and check the answers, so independent experts may decline to credit the insight mainly to the machine.

rows.line: Sam Altman wrote that 2026 would likely bring AI systems able to work out genuinely new insights.

judgement.reason: The wording is modest: robots able to carry out tasks in the real world. From general knowledge, general-purpose robots are already in paid pilots in factories and warehouses, and extending that through 2027 makes paid work outside test sites probable, at small scale. The case against is that most deployments remain supervised, narrow and closer to demonstrations than to real jobs, so a strict reading of general-purpose could fail.

rows.line: Sam Altman said 2027 may bring robots able to carry out tasks in the real world.

judgement.reason: Extending the fast growth in task length and the early signs of AI doing AI research puts expert-level systems around the early part of the next decade, with something clearly superhuman a few years after. That places the end of 2035 near the middle of a wide spread, so there is no honest lean. Against it stand limits on compute, power and experiments; for it, the trend has kept beating forecasts and research automation could shorten the last stretch.

rows.line: Sam Altman wrote that superintelligence might arrive within a few thousand days, though it could take longer, and said he is confident it will come.

judgement.reason: The definition asks for Nobel-level work across fields with autonomous multi-week tasks by the middle of 2028. Extending the reliable-horizon trend that far reaches tasks of some weeks at best, in software, on clean benchmark tasks, and that is far from Nobel-level science across fields; no system that learns continually on the job has shipped. Amodei himself called it closer to an even bet and conditional on scaling holding. The trend running faster than its past rate is the main thing that could prove this wrong.

rows.line: If scaling continues, AI as able as a country of geniuses arrives within a year or two.

judgement.reason: By the end of 2036 the task-length trend has a decade to run, and even a marked slowdown would carry reliable autonomous work from hours to many months. Expert-level autonomous systems across most fields by then look more likely than not, though not as near certain as his odds claim. The strongest doubts are that expert legal work is still rarely completed end to end today, and that on-the-job learning and reliability on long tasks may need new ideas and not just scale.

Extending the horizon trend gets agents to well-specified projects of weeks by then, not to choosing research directions. The case for it is that labs see their own best systems months early and report rapid gains.

rows.line: Leopold Aschenbrenner called it strikingly plausible that models could do the job of the engineers and researchers who build AI by 2027.

judgement.reason: A drop-in remote worker at the level of leading experts needs long, messy, open-ended work done reliably, and today's best models complete only a small share of expert legal tasks end to end. Extending the reliable-horizon trend to the end of 2028 gives tasks of months on benchmark-style work, which is promising but leaves memory, on-the-job learning and judgement unsolved. I put this at well under even odds; the trend holding at its recent fast pace is the main thing that would make it true.

judgement.reason: Judged as whether AI can do any remote job by about 2040, this looks more likely than not. The task-length trend would need to slow dramatically for agents not to handle months-long work by then, and remote jobs need no robotics. The case against is that the last few tasks in a job, and cost parity on them, may take far longer than the first.

The strongest objection is that progress so far has been smooth and bound by compute and experiments, which could stretch the climb.

rows.line: Nick Bostrom judged it unlikely that the climb from human-level AI to superintelligence would take decades, and more likely that it would be fast or moderate.

judgement.reason: Judged as whether superintelligence exists by the end of 2033, I lean no, which agrees with his less than even odds. Expert-level systems look likely around the early part of the next decade, and greatly outperforming the best people in nearly every field should take some years more. The fast task-length trend is the main reason this could arrive sooner than I expect.

rows.line: Nick Bostrom clarified that, all things considered, he gave less than even odds that superintelligence would be developed by 2033.

judgement.reason: Commercial agents already plan, act toward goals and show some awareness of their situation, and capability on long tasks has been rising fast. With more than a generation left, systems meeting his bar at acceptable cost look very probable, likely well before the date. Only a deep and lasting stall, or a deliberate global halt, would prevent it.

rows.line: Joe Carlsmith gave about two chances in three that advanced, agentic, strategically aware AI becomes possible and affordable to build by 2070.

judgement.reason: Judged as whether the catastrophe occurs by 2070, it is unlikely, in line with his own low odds. That rests on general knowledge: permanent disempowerment needs misaligned systems to escape many layers of testing, oversight and rival systems at once. The serious counterweight is that oversight has not been tried against systems more capable than people, and labs' own safety pauses show the worry is taken seriously.

judgement.reason: Frontier systems already match people on many expert tests and the length of task they finish keeps growing fast, so human-level ability across the board before 2100 looks very probable. rows.line: David Chalmers put his credence in human-level AI before 2100 at more than one half, while saying he would be surprised to see it within the next thirty years.

judgement.reason: AI able to direct engineering on that scale implies mature superintelligence plus mastery of physical industry. By 2030 that is very unlikely, and by 2040 I put it below even odds, close to his own figures, because superhuman systems look likely only in the middle of the next decade and industrial know-how takes longer. This rests on general knowledge. Fast takeoff once research is automated is what could make the 2040 mark.

rows.line: Paul Christiano put about one chance in seven on AI able to build a Dyson sphere by 2030, and about two chances in five by 2040.

judgement.reason: A true explosion on fixed compute needs returns to software research to stay high as the easy gains go, and frontier progress has so far leaned heavily on ever larger training runs and experiments. I put the odds a little under even. The lab's own figures show agents already doing much research work, and algorithmic efficiency has improved quickly, which is the best case for the other side.

rows.line: Paul Christiano gave even odds on whether an intelligence explosion driven by software improvements alone is possible at all.

judgement.reason: Reward hacking and proxy gaming are real and growing, so the early part of his story is visible. The settling test is stronger: key institutions run by systems that people can no longer correct, and I think institutions will notice and correct enough of this, helped by partial progress on alignment. The worry is that correction gets harder as systems outpace their overseers and as competition punishes those who slow down.

rows.line: Paul Christiano expected that, without solving intent alignment, AI failure would come as a gradual loss of human steering to optimised proxies, possibly ending in a sudden cascade.

judgement.reason: Judged as whether transformative AI arrives by about 2050, this looks very probable, and likely much earlier than her median. Training compute has grown far faster than the report assumed and capability has outrun its anchors. So the by-date claim holds while the timing looks too cautious. Slow diffusion into the physical economy is the main reason it could still take until mid-century.

rows.line: Ajeya Cotra gave about one chance in ten that AI fully automates AI research and development, matching human researchers, by the end of 2026.

judgement.reason: The claim needs people to lose control of the economy and politics in the next decade and then to be gone by 2050. Some drift of decisions to machines is plausible, and labour's share of income is softening, but extinction by 2050 through gradual ceding requires every major society to fail to react over decades. The pull of competition toward handing over control is the strongest point on his side.

judgement.reason: Judged as AI able to automate essentially all cognitive work by 2043, this looks more likely than not, and probably earlier than his median. The task-length trend and compute growth have both run ahead of the model's assumptions. The by-2030 part of his spread still looks unlikely to me. What cuts against is the long tail of tasks needing judgement, trust and learning on the job.

rows.line: Tom Davidson's takeoff model put a median of 2043 on AI able to readily automate all cognitive work, with about one chance in ten by 2030 and four in five by 2070.

judgement.reason: By the time AI matches professionals on the last hold-out tasks it will already be far ahead on most, which favours a short gap. But the step to far surpassing people needs experiments, compute and real-world feedback, and I expect those to stretch it to a few years, the same view taken on the other takeoff forecasts here. The lab's research figures are self-reported and still show people closely involved, so this is a moderate lean resting mostly on general reasoning.

rows.line: Daniel Kokotajlo's August 2026 median for AI that matches or exceeds the best human experts on almost every cognitive task is November 2028.

judgement.reason: The claim is conditional on AI continuing to displace people from work, thought and consent across economy, culture and state, and that condition does most of the work. Early softening in labour's share and a rising automation share of AI use fit the first steps, but say nothing about whether societies respond. I see no basis to lean on whether voters and states keep decisive roles once the condition holds.

rows.line: Jan Kulveit and co-authors argue that if AI keeps displacing human labour, thought and consent across economy, culture and state, humans will probably lose effective control without any takeover.

judgement.reason: Judged as machine intelligence clearly outstripping humanity's combined intellect by about 2045, I lean yes. If expert-level systems arrive in the early part of the next decade, a further decade of copying, speeding up and improving them plausibly gets there. The capability trend so far supports the early steps. Physical limits on power and chips, or a political brake, are the strongest reasons it could miss.

rows.line: Ray Kurzweil set 2045 as the year of the Singularity, when machine intelligence created by people would vastly exceed all human intelligence combined.

judgement.reason: Chatbots already fool ordinary judges in short tests, and three more years of progress in memory and consistency should handle long expert questioning when a model is tuned to imitate a person. This rests on general knowledge. The real risk is procedural: the formal test under the bet's rules has to be run, and determined expert judges may still find tells.

rows.line: Ray Kurzweil bet publicly that a machine would pass a rigorous Turing test, judged under formal rules with expert interrogators, by 2029.

judgement.reason: Systems built mainly on language models keep gaining abilities he said they lacked, including abstract reasoning, where top scores are now very high. I expect systems still recognisably of that family, with added memory and learning, to reach human level. His best ground is that learning on the job has reached only a middle rung in production, and if the fix is a new architecture he could claim to be right.

rows.line: Eli Lifland's August 2026 median for an automated coder, an AI that labs would rather keep than their human coders, is January 2030.

judgement.reason: This date sits close to my own central guess for top-expert AI, so I cannot honestly lean. The task-length trend and very high abstract-reasoning scores argue for sooner; unsolved on-the-job learning, reliability on messy work and the slow tail of hard tasks argue for later. rows.line: Eli Lifland's August 2026 median for AI that matches or exceeds the best human experts on almost every cognitive task is July 2032.

judgement.reason: By the lab's own count agents already put in more research workdays than its people, though with heavy supervision, and the task-length trend has two decades to run before the deadline. AI research effort matching the human research workforce by 2045 looks very probable, and within a decade is plausible. The outside trial that found no developer speed-up is the main caution, and it argues for delay more than for failure.

judgement.reason: This is the weaker cousin of a full software explosion: any accelerating growth from AI improving its own software. Agents now carry much lab research by the lab's own count, which favours it, while diminishing returns and the need for compute-heavy experiments weigh against it. With no independent reading of research speed on fixed compute, even odds is a fair summary and I have no better lean.

judgement.reason: Walking is close to solved, dexterity is improving quickly with learned control, and language models already handle much social interaction. With more than two decades left and strong AI help in robot design likely along the way, matching people in ordinary settings by 2048 looks more likely than not. This rests on general knowledge. Hands, touch and cheap reliable hardware have resisted progress for decades, which is the real risk.

judgement.reason: Judged on the claim as worded: limits outside the lab, such as experiments, regulation, liability and the pace at which organisations change, keep binding through 2030 even if agents come to do most research inside labs. I expect that, with diffusion indicators staying near ordinary ranges, and the gap between the headline horizon and the reliable one fits slow real-world use. The site's narrower check at the invention stage may well go against the authors before then, if outside tests confirm agents doing more research work than people.

Given that condition, a robot population growing by its own size within a year is plausible, since factories can be turned to robot production much as car plants were turned to arms in wartime, and young industries already grow that fast from small bases. judgement.reason: The claim is conditional and absolute: superintelligence built with methods like today's kills everyone. High-bandwidth memory was sold out well ahead, memory prices rose sharply, and advanced packaging capacity remained allocated despite expansion. judgement.reason: The cheapest price for an hour of model-equivalent work is already very low and falling, so cost does not look like the binding limit for most office tasks. Running many agents at once could raise the bill enough to matter for the hardest tasks, which is where the claim has force.

judgement.reason: By the lab's own count agents do much research work, yet people still intervene on about as many long tasks as not, and nothing independent shows research itself speeding up. The projects span design, video and other multi-tool work where agents remain weak, which tips me against the date, on general knowledge.

Power and equipment supply are tighter limits than labour on many sites, and a spending slowdown would end the shortage quickly.

judgement.reason: Rests on general knowledge, not a site reading. Payment networks and banks already ask who authorised a purchase an agent made, and agents still act through a person's own login, which leaves weak records. Once real sums move this way, disputes over who answers for a bad transaction look hard to avoid. The strongest point against is that card rules and signed mandates may settle liability quietly before it ever binds.

rows.line: Proof of what an AI agent (a model that carries out tasks with software tools on a person's behalf) did, and who answers for it, becomes a bottleneck once agents handle money.

judgement.reason: Rests on general knowledge. The loud cases are blocks, such as the largest online retailer suing a browser agent and social networks barring scrapers, but under a single counting rule the quieter openings look more numerous: shops, payment firms and travel sites have signed up to agent checkout and tool protocols through 2025 and 2026. The strongest point against is that most of these openings admit only chosen partners on the platform's own terms, which a strict reading could score as a fence.

rows.line: Large platforms move to keep outside agents off them more often than they let them in.
rows.settles: Platforms opening to outside agents more often than they block them, counted under one rule for both; this site's hand-kept ledger does not yet sweep both sides that way, so it tests nothing yet.

judgement.reason: Rests on general knowledge. Cover sold specifically for AI failures is still a tiny line in 2026, and the larger move among insurers this year has been to add AI exclusions to standard policies, not to price the risk. Cyber cover took well over a decade to reach comparable size, so this would need a much faster climb in the years left before 2032. The strongest point against is that loose definitions could let AI-related premium inside cyber and liability policies be counted toward the total.

rows.line: Insurers write several billion dollars a year of cover for AI's failures worldwide by 2032 [cite:deloitte_ai_insurance].

judgement.reason: Rests on general knowledge. In law, coding and finance the pattern so far is that each new general release overtakes models tuned for the field, and the best-known legal start-up dropped its own tuned model for the labs' general ones. Extending that pattern is the basis of the call. The strongest point against is that in biology, robotics, speech and other areas where the data is not text on the web, purpose-built models still lead, and that set of exceptions may prove wider than a few regulated niches.

rows.line: Start-ups that build a model for one field fall behind as the labs' general models improve, outside a few regulated niches where data is scarce.
rows.settles: Models built for one field keeping their lead over each new general release.

judgement.reason: The largest expert-data seller's revenue has grown several times over in a year, but by press accounts that growth comes from a handful of labs, so the site's reading shows a bigger market, not a broader one. Firms outside the labs mostly lack the research staff to turn bought data into a better model, and they can rent the result instead. The strongest point against is that large software firms and banks have begun buying test sets and practice tasks to check agents, which could grow into real spending with no date to miss.

Purpose-built AI policies already exist from a large reinsurer and from several start-ups backed by established underwriters, and as standard policies gain AI exclusions, buyers who deploy agents are pushed toward separate cover. That makes the weaker claim of real sale to large buyers more likely than not, even though the multi-year premium forecast for 2032 looks too high. The strongest point against is that take-up so far is small and large buyers may simply self-insure or lean on vendor indemnities.

judgement.reason: The site's count shows three announced brakes at one lab in the past year, including a release gated behind safeguards, and from general knowledge another leading lab has kept its strongest model to a limited set of partners in 2026 on security grounds. Gaps between a model being trained and being sold openly seem to be widening as cyber and biology risk thresholds are reached. The strongest point against is that these are the labs' own accounts, the paused run restarted within a month, and commercial rivalry punishes whoever waits longest, so 'loosely in step' is the fragile part.

Further training has become much cheaper, and a few of the biggest coding apps do train their own small models, yet they still send their hardest work to the labs' best models because users pay for quality at the frontier. As long as each new general release moves that frontier, owning a tuned model saves money only on routine calls. The strongest point against is that routine calls are most of the volume, so a quiet shift of the bulk of traffic to in-house models could satisfy the forecast while the frontier is still rented.

rows.line: If training a model further on a firm's own work keeps getting cheaper, apps train their own instead of renting the best.

The three kinds of firm named have different customers today: the data sellers earn nearly all their money from the labs, the hosts sell computing to developers, and only the custom trainers already do the forecast business. Some overlap is appearing, as hosts add training services, but a full merging into one business needs enterprise demand for tuned open models that has so far stayed modest. The strongest point against is that data sellers facing concentrated lab customers have a strong motive to move toward enterprises.

rows.line: Leading firms that host models, sell training data or do custom training, such as Baseten, Mercor and Applied Compute, converge on one business, tuning open models for firms and selling them the use.

The agent failures seen so far, such as deleted databases, wrong purchases and agents tricked by hidden instructions, trace to agents doing the work badly or being manipulated, and the first large market failure seems likely to be reported the same way. An inability to check what an agent did usually deepens a loss instead of starting it, so the public account will tend to blame skill or security. The strongest point against is that fraud by agents nobody can identify is exactly a checking failure, and that may well come first where money is involved.

Models become nearly as reliable on long jobs as on short ones, and not just because the tests have run out of longer tasks. Most of the labour-market trackers we follow break at the same time. And either the share of work hours done with AI passes a fifth, or productivity runs well above trend for years on end.

The strongest point against is that reliable agents able to work unsupervised for days would be a leap of the kind denied here, and coding tools already showed adoption moving within months of a capability step.

The strongest point against is that the stricter test, employment falling as coding tools spread, is close to being met already, and agents that finish whole projects could turn a flat line into a clear decline.

The strongest point against is that time saved inside firms does show up as measured productivity when the same output needs fewer paid hours, so 'most' may overstate the miss.

rows.line: Workers stop sharing the gains
rows.settles: The case that workers share in AI's gains fails if the typical full-time worker's pay, after inflation, sits below its level at the end of 2022, just before ChatGPT, for four quarters running while the economy's output keeps growing. Pascual Restrepo, an economist who models work once machines can do every task, finds that workers' total pay never falls below its level before such AI unless something else, such as market power over computing, gets in the way; the typical worker's pay is the nearest measure this site reads.

judgement.reason: The site's count of circular financing is very large and still rising, and the leading chip maker has taken stakes in labs and smaller clouds and backed their capacity, which gives it a say over who gets chips. That practice looks set to continue while supply is short and its cash pile grows. The weakness is the test itself: almost all of its revenue is still plain hardware sales, and the stakes are equity rather than a share of customers' income, so a strict reading could go against Hobart.

rests_on.name: Circular financing scale

rows.line: NVIDIA keeps financing its own customers in return for a share of their income, and uses such deals to gain a say over who gets computing capacity.
rows.settles: NVIDIA's revenue staying almost wholly one-off sales of hardware.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge. Power and building shells, not chips, have become the binding shortage, and at least one large cloud chief has already said publicly that chips were waiting for powered space. As chip output keeps rising faster than grid connections, more of this is likely. The counterpoint is that chips lose value quickly, so buyers have every reason to delay orders or redirect them to sites that are ready rather than let them sit.

rows.line: The cloud companies start storing new chips instead of installing them, the sign Cahn watches for that data centres are running late [cite:cahn_2025].
rows.settles: New chips going into service as fast as they arrive.

judgement.reason: The number of active sellers of training environments in the site's directory is still rising, and labs deliberately spread purchases across many specialists by field of expertise. Nothing so far suggests one or two sellers handling most of what the frontier labs buy. The strongest point against is that the largest expert-data firms are growing much faster than the rest, and labs may bring more of this work in-house or buy the sellers, which would thin the field.

rests_on.name: Active RL-environment vendors (directory count)

rows.line: The market for training data stays split among many specialist sellers rather than gathering around one or two.
rows.settles: One or two sellers coming to handle most of what the frontier labs buy.

rows.line: Work that must be decided faster than a message can reach a data centre, or on little power, is run on the spot, whoever holds the knowledge.
rows.settles: Time-critical work such as driving and industrial control moving to distant data centres as networks improve.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge. Small models keep getting better and some simple work, such as dictation and autocomplete, does run on phones and laptops. But the everyday uses that are growing fastest are long agent tasks and search-backed answers, which need the largest models and far more memory than personal devices have. The best case for Paik is that privacy and cost push routine requests onto devices once small open models are good enough for most of them.

rows.line: Much of AI's everyday work moves out of distant data centres onto people's own phones and laptops.
rows.settles: Everyday use staying in cloud data centres as capable open models get smaller.

judgement.reason: The estimated gross margin of the frontier labs sits far below that of classic software, and the labs recoup well under what they spend. Both readings are old or rough, and the main drag today is the cost of compute rather than deployment staff, so Hobart's mechanism is only part of the story. Still, the labs are hiring engineers to work inside customers at pace, and the claim fails only if labs report software-like margins while doing so, which looks unlikely for some years.

rests_on.name: Frontier lab gross margin (estimated)
Lab recoupment ratio

rows.line: The labs' margins are pulled down because the staff who deploy their models grow with their customers, which a pure software business avoids.
rows.settles: Labs reporting gross margins at or above classic software's while running large teams inside their customers.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge of press reports, not a site reading. In 2026 the two leading labs each launched a deployment and services venture with private-equity backers, one of them under the lab's own name, and each venture has since bought a consultancy. On the launch wording the forecast looks close to met already, with two years left. The doubt is ownership: at least one lab is reported to hold only a minority of its venture, and whether either holds a majority is not established, so a strict reading that demands control could still go the other way.

rows.line: A frontier lab launches or majority-owns a professional services firm, under its own brand or at arm's length, by September 2028.
A frontier lab, or a company it controls, comes to own an ordinary operating business in a licensed trade by the end of 2028.

judgement.reason: The site's count of purchases and team hires by labs and compute companies over the trailing year rose at each of the last three readings, and public listings remain rare for small data and tooling firms. Extending that rise even modestly makes being bought the common way out. The caveats are real: part of the rise reflects a more thorough search, one buyer accounts for much of it, and a funding squeeze at the labs would stop the buying quickly.

rests_on.name: Lab vertical integration (acquisitions and acquihires, trailing four quarters)

rows.line: Being bought by a lab or a compute company becomes the usual way out for the start-ups that sell them data and tools.
rows.settles: The yearly count flattening, read only over quarters searched the same way. A later search that turns up deals missed earlier also raises the count, so it is not by itself a sign of more buying.

judgement.reason: The labs are plainly buying more from the layer that supplies training inputs, and the expert-data market has grown very quickly. Records of real work from leading applications are scarcer and harder to copy than generic practice environments, whose sellers keep multiplying, which usually means falling prices. The main doubt is whether leading app companies will sell their records at all, since many see them as their own advantage against the labs.

rests_on.name: Expert-data market run-rate (Mercor)
Labs buying from the training-input layer (enter bell)

rows.line: Labs buy more of their training data straight from leading app companies and specialists, squeezing the firms that sell general practice environments.
rows.settles: General environment sellers keeping their share of the labs' data budgets.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge. The labs do differ, with some stronger in coding and business use and others with consumers, but those differences come from product focus and model quality, not from purchased business records. General models have so far kept beating specialist ones in fields such as law and medicine. Hobart hedged the claim with a may, and it could still come true if exclusive data deals in a regulated trade give one lab a lasting edge there.

rows.line: The leading labs may pull apart by industry, each strongest where it has bought the most specialist business records.
rows.settles: The labs staying interchangeable in every industry, with none ahead in a trade because of the data it bought.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge. Over the past two years the top place on the main measures has passed back and forth among three labs, sometimes within months, and no lab has held it for several years running. Compute split between serving customers and training the next model is a fair account of why. The risk is that AI doing its own research lets one lab compound a lead, which is exactly what the labs themselves are betting on.

rows.line: The lab with the best model keeps changing, because the leader uses its chips to serve its popular model while rivals train the next one.
rows.settles: One lab keeping the best model for several years running.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge of how supply chains behave. The claim needs only one squeezed part to turn, and memory, older chips for rent and optical parts all have long histories of shortage followed by glut once new plants open. Rental prices for older chips have already eased at times. The claim would fail only if every scarce link stayed scarce, which would be without precedent in semiconductors.

rows.line: Somewhere along the chip supply chain, a part AI has made scarce proves easier to expand than expected, and its price turns.
rows.settles: Every part squeezed by AI's demand staying scarce and rising in price.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge. The largest consumer lab already earns most of its revenue from subscriptions, and the labs are pushing coding tools, seats and deployment by their own engineers because margins and loyalty are better there. The counterweight is that agents consume enormous volumes of tokens, so metered access could keep growing as fast as products do, and much product revenue is itself billed by use. This is a claim about where revenue comes from, not about customers being tied down, which is judged separately.

rows.line: The labs earn a growing share of their revenue from products and deployments inside their customers' firms rather than from selling access to their models by the token.
rows.settles: The labs' revenue staying mostly in selling access to their models by the token.

judgement.reason: The only site reading on firms using more than one model is several years old, so this rests mostly on general knowledge. Businesses routinely route work across several labs, switching a model behind an application takes little effort, and bans on copying models have proved hard to enforce. This sits alongside the view that labs earn more from products: product revenue can grow without binding customers. The strongest point against is that memory, stored context and workflow tools built around one lab raise the cost of leaving over time.

rests_on.name: Enterprise multi-model usage share (Menlo)

rows.line: Labs' efforts to tie customers down, through exclusive deals and bans on copying their models, eventually fail, and moving between labs stays cheap.
rows.settles: Customers becoming bound to one lab by exclusive deals and bans on copying.

judgement.reason: This rests mostly on general knowledge. Buyers still choose models on quality, speed, reliability and the kinds of input handled, and pay large premiums for the best one in coding, which is not how anyone buys electricity. The case against is that for routine tasks many models are now good enough, and that part of the market already buys on price alone.

rows.line: Models keep differing in efficiency and in the kinds of input they handle, so they do not become an interchangeable utility like electricity.
rows.settles: Buyers treating models as interchangeable and choosing on the price of a token alone.

judgement.reason: The gap between open and closed models is small on the site's index, yet businesses' use of open models has stayed a small share, because renting the frontier is easier and general models improve faster than a firm can retrain its own. Supplying a model with a firm's documents at the moment of use has largely replaced training on them. Every firm is a very strong claim. It could yet come true in a looser sense if cheap tuning becomes a standard feature that the labs offer on their own models.

rests_on.name: Open-weights gap to the closed frontier (ECI points)

rows.line: Every firm ends up with a model of its own, trained on its own work.
rows.settles: Businesses' use of open models, the easiest kind to make one's own, falling further.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge. Agents need an authoritative store of customers, money and staff to act on, and firms very rarely rip out such systems, so their customer losses should stay lower than those of lighter tools that an agent can rebuild. The strongest evidence against is that investors marked down record-keeping software alongside everything else in 2026, fearing that agents turn it into a cheap database beneath someone else's product.

rows.line: Coding agents slow new firms' purchases of ready-made software but make the programs that hold a business's core records worth more.
rows.settles: Software that holds a business's records losing customers as fast as other software.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge. The largest technology firms already rent large amounts of computing to labs that compete with their own models, and at least one lab now rents from a rival model maker. The claim fails only if the big firms keep all their capacity for themselves, which is the opposite of what they are doing. Whether the capacity is truly spare, rather than built to order for those tenants, is the part that remains open.

rows.line: The largest technology firms build more computing than they need and rent the spare to rivals, so the industry becomes one shared bet on demand for AI.
rows.settles: The largest firms keeping their computing for their own use and renting none of it out.

judgement.reason: Open models trail the closed frontier only narrowly on the site's index, yet most businesses still rent, because running models well needs scarce chips, power and skilled staff, and rented models improve without effort from the buyer. Most businesses do not even run their own email servers. The exceptions are real: defence, banks and firms in countries wary of foreign suppliers will host their own, but they are a minority.

rests_on.name: Open-weights gap to the closed frontier (ECI points)

rows.line: Most businesses end up running models on machines they control rather than renting a lab's.
rows.settles: Businesses sticking with rented frontier models even as open models improve.

rows.line: A model of a firm's own pays only where the firm senses something no one else can; elsewhere a system trained on many firms' results does better.
rows.settles: Systems tuned on a firm's own history beating pooled ones in trades where no firm senses anything scarce. The only evidence so far is its author's own simulation.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge. Governments have already taken equity in a leading chip maker and in suppliers of critical minerals, and state-owned funds in the Gulf and Asia hold stakes in labs and data-centre builders. The trend is towards more of this as AI is treated as a strategic industry. The claim would fail only if states went back to being lenders and customers alone, and a change of government could slow new stakes but would not undo existing ones.

rows.line: Governments take direct stakes in the companies that make chips, power and models.
rows.settles: States staying lenders and buyers rather than owners.

judgement.reason: The test is whether AI firms' profits grow as fast as the value users get. In level, users are far ahead: the survey estimate of user value for one country alone is large and rising, while the labs make losses and competition among several similar models keeps prices down. What cuts the other way is that chip makers' profits have lately grown at least as fast as the survey estimate, so a strict reading of the growth test could go against the claim, and a single lab pulling ahead could price accordingly. This differs from the site's other test on user value, which sets one country's consumer survey against worldwide revenue, a far easier bar for sellers to clear.

rests_on.name: Consumer surplus from generative AI (willingness to accept)

rows.line: The people who use AI keep far more of its value than the firms that make it.
rows.settles: AI firms' profits growing as fast as the value their users get.

judgement.reason: This rests on general knowledge. Once a narrow task is done reliably, firms move it to small cheap models or to ordinary code written by an agent, and the price of a given level of capability has fallen steeply every year. Spending on that task then stops growing. What keeps total spending rising is that cheaper tasks get run far more and new harder tasks keep arriving, so the pattern may be hard to see outside individual tasks.

rows.line: Much narrow work AI does is turned into cheap fixed routines, so spending on each such task rises for a while and then stops.
rows.settles: Spending on well-defined tasks staying high after they are solved.
